result:
The proposed answer is wrong. A limiting probability must lie in $[0,1]$, but $\lambda \in (0,\infty)$ can be any positive number, so the answer $\lambda$ is impossible whenever $\lambda > 1$.

A standard approach gives the right answer. Write $G$ for a $k \times n$ generator matrix of $C$. Then $C$ is MDS if and only if every $k$ columns of $G$ are linearly independent, i.e., every $k \times k$ column-submatrix is invertible. There are $\binom{n}{k}$ such column subsets. For a uniformly random $G$, each $k \times k$ submatrix is singular with probability about $1/q$. So the expected number of singular subsets is about $\binom{n}{k}/q \to \lambda$. When $k/n \to 0$, these bad events are approximately independent, so the number of bad subsets is approximately Poisson with mean $\lambda$. The probability of zero bad subsets therefore tends to $e^{-\lambda}$.

I did not verify this against a cited theorem, so treat $e^{-\lambda}$ as the heuristic (Poisson) limit rather than a checked result. Either way, the proposed answer $\lambda$ cannot be correct, and its justification is hand-waving.

VERDICT: REJECT
